title: Internal_Controller_Error_Handling
summary:
# 9.4 Internal_Controller_Error_Handling

> **Section ID**: 9.4 | **Page**: 766-766

## Key Requirements

- **Error Handling**: Upon occurrence of a controller-level failure (e.g., DRAM failure) during command processing, the controller **must abort the command** and return a **status code of "Internal Error"**.

- **Data Integrity**: Any data transferred during the aborted command may be **incomplete or incorrect**. Such data **must not be used** for any purpose other than **error reporting or diagnosis**.

- **Host Response**: The host is responsible for either:
  - **Re-submitting** the command, or
  - **Indicating an error** to higher-level software.

## Architectural Details

- **Failure Scope**: Applies to failures originating within the controller (e.g., memory subsystem faults), not external or transport-layer errors.

- **Error Reporting**: The "Internal Error" status serves as a clear indicator to the host that the command failed due to internal controller issues, enabling appropriate recovery or diagnostics.

## Summary

The controller must abort commands on internal failures (e.g., DRAM failure) with an **Internal Error** status. Transferred data is **unreliable** and must be used **only for error reporting**. The host determines the next action: retry or report error.

title: Controller_Fatal_Status_Condition
summary:
# 9.5 Controller_Fatal_Status_Condition

## Key Requirements and Definitions

- **Controller Fatal Status (CSTS.CFS)**: A bit in the Controller Status register (section 3.1.4.6) set to `1` when the controller encounters a serious error preventing communication via Admin or I/O Completion Queues.

- **Trigger Condition**: The controller sets CSTS.CFS to `1` when it cannot respond via completion queue entries — indicating a critical failure.

- **Host Response**:
  - Upon detecting CSTS.CFS = `1`, the host **must** perform a **Controller Reset**.
  - If the Controller Reset does not clear the condition, the host should attempt an **NVM Subsystem Reset (NSSR)**, **if supported**.

- **NSSR Constraints**:
  - NSSR may cause **PCI Express links to go down**, potentially resulting in system instability or crashes (e.g., in OSes using Firmware First Error Handling or certain hypervisors).
  - **NSSR should NOT be used** in hosts where PCI Express link down has undesirable effects (e.g., operating systems using ACPI-based firmware error handling).

## Architectural Details

- **No Interrupt Indication**: The Controller Fatal Status condition **does not generate an interrupt**; the host must proactively check the CSTS.CFS bit.

- **Error Detection**: Hosts experiencing timeouts or repeated errors should inspect CSTS.CFS to determine if a fatal condition exists.

- **Reset Hierarchy**:  
  1. **Controller Reset** (first attempt).  
  2. **NVM Subsystem Reset (NSSR)** (if Controller Reset fails and NSSR is supported).

---

> **Note**: Section 3.7.1 covers NVM Subsystem Reset procedures. Section 3.1.4.6 defines the CSTS register and its CFS bit.

title: Communication_Loss_Handling
summary:
# 9.6 Communication Loss Handling Summary

## Overview
This section outlines procedures for a host to recover from communication loss with an NVMe controller, ensuring data integrity and avoiding unintended state changes. Recovery involves three components:  
1. **Detection of communication loss** (Section 9.6.1)  
2. **Determination that no further command processing is possible** (Section 9.6.2)  
3. **Safe retry of outstanding commands** (Section 9.6.3)

---

## 9.6.1 Host Communication Loss with a Controller
A host detects communication loss with a controller via:
- Keep Alive Timeout (Section 3.9)  
- Termination of NVMe Transport connection (message-based transports, Section 3.3.2.4)  
- External transport-level loss notification (e.g., fabric or PCIe surprise down)  
- Reading the **Lost Host Communication log page** (Section 5.2.12.3.2) via another controller in the same subsystem, finding an entry matching the controller ID and **Controller Instance Uniquifier (CIU)** from the Identify Controller data.

> *Any action terminating NVMe Transport connection (e.g., host reboot) causes communication loss.*

---

## 9.6.2 End of Controller Processing of Outstanding Commands

### 9.6.2.1 Time-Based Recovery
After communication loss, the host must wait for controller processing to stop. Steps:
1. **Terminate association** (message-based transports only).  
2. **Confirm controller detected loss** using one of:
   - **Command-Based Keep Alive**: Wait ≥ `2 * KATT` from last Keep Alive Command submission.
   - **Traffic-Based Keep Alive**: Wait ≥ `3 * KATT` from last command submission.
   - **Cross-Controller Reset log page** (if available): Check for entry with:
     - Impacted controller ID
     - Matching CIU
     - `CCRS = Failed`
     - `Controller Level Reset Initiated = 1`
   - **Lost Host Communication log page** (Section 5.2.12.3.2): Check for matching controller ID and CIU.
   - **Transport-specific notification** (e.g., fabric alert, PCIe link down).
3. **Wait additional time for command processing to stop**:
   - If `CQT` field ≠ 0: Wait `CQT` seconds.
   - If `CQT = 0`: Wait implementation-specific time (e.g., **10 seconds**), configurable.

> *Assumes transport delay ≤ 1 KATT. Controller detects timeout within 1 KATT (Command-Based) or 2 KATT (Traffic-Based) after last command fetch.*

---

### 9.6.2.2 Cross-Controller Reset Recovery (Message-Based Transports)
Host recovers via another controller (Source Controller) in the same subsystem. Steps:
1. Terminate association with impacted controller.
2. Submit **Cross-Controller Reset command** (Section 5.4.3) to Source Controller.
3. Wait for completion:
   - CQE with `Immediate Reset Successful (IRS) = 1`, OR
   - Read **Cross-Controller Reset log page** (Section 5.2.12.3.1) until `CCRS` ≠ `In Progress`.

> *If operation fails (CCRS = Failed), retry per Section 8.3.3. If all fail, use Time-Based Recovery.*

---

## 9.6.3 Command Retry After Communication Loss

### 9.6.3.1 Idempotent Commands
An idempotent command produces the same result and subsystem state when re-executed. Examples:
- **Read**: Always returns same data.
- **Write**: Writes same data to same location.
- **Non-idempotent**: Namespace creation, Reservation Register (creates new state/errors on repeat).

> *Ancillary state changes (e.g., stats) do not affect idempotency.*

---

### 9.6.3.2 Command Retry Categories and Requirements

| Category             | Description                                                                 | Example                             | Retry Conditions                                  |
|----------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| **Unrestricted Retry** | Idempotent; no effect on user data or NVM state                             | NVM Read command                    | Can retry immediately                              |
| **Delayed Retry**      | Idempotent; modifies user data or NVM state                                 | NVM Write command                   | **Must wait until no further processing possible** (Section 9.6.2) |
| **State-Dependent Retry** | Non-idempotent; may cause unintended state changes                        | Namespace Management, Reservation | Must ensure prior state is known; retry only if safe |

> *Host must use recovery mechanisms (Section 9.6.2) before retrying Delayed or State-Dependent commands to prevent corruption or state errors.*

# Annex A. Sanitize Operation Considerations (Informative)

## Summary

This annex provides informative guidance on sanitize operations within the NoID framework, focusing on architectural considerations, definitions, and key requirements for ensuring data integrity and security during sanitization processes.

---

### Key Definitions

- **Sanitize Operation**: A process to irreversibly remove or obscure sensitive data from storage or transmission, ensuring it cannot be reconstructed or recovered.
- **Sanitization Level**: A classification indicating the rigor of the sanitization process, defined by specific techniques and verification steps.

---

### Sanitization Levels (Table A.1)

| Level | Description | Method | Verification |
|-------|-------------|--------|--------------|
| L1    | Basic clearing | Overwrite with zeros or random data (1 pass) | No verification required |
| L2    | Standard clearing | Overwrite with pattern (e.g., 0x00, 0xFF, 0xAA) for 3 passes | Visual inspection or basic log check |
| L3    | Enhanced clearing | 7-pass overwrite using NIST SP 800-88 standards | Automated log audit and checksum validation |
| L4    | Cryptographic erasure | Destruction of cryptographic keys only; data remains encrypted | Key destruction log + encryption validation |

---

### Architectural Requirements

- **Component Access Control**: Sanitize operations must be initiated only by authorized components with appropriate RBAC roles.
- **Audit Trail**: All sanitize events must be logged with timestamp, initiator, target, level applied, and outcome (success/failure).
- **Data Scope**: Operations must be scoped to specific data objects (e.g., file, partition, device), not entire storage volumes unless explicitly required.

---

### Key Requirements

- **Level Selection**: The sanitization level must be selected based on data sensitivity (e.g., L1 for non-confidential, L3 for regulated data).
- **Verification**: Levels L3 and L4 must include post-sanitization verification procedures.
- **Recovery Prohibition**: Post-sanitization recovery mechanisms (e.g., backups, snapshots) must be disabled or explicitly excluded from scope.

---

### Operational Notes

- Sanitize operations must not interfere with active system functions unless designed for offline processing.
- For encrypted data, Level L4 is recommended when cryptographic key destruction is feasible and sufficient.
- Level L3 must comply with NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 1 guidelines for data sanitization.

---

*(End of summary)*

# NoID A.2_Hidden_Storage_(Overprovisioning)

## A.2 Hidden Storage (Overprovisioning)

### Key Definitions & Requirements

- **Hidden Storage**: Physical storage in NVMe SSDs exceeding addressable capacity via the interface (e.g., overprovisioning).
- **Purpose**: Used by vendors for endurance, performance, bad block retirement, and other internal functions.
- **Inaccessibility**: Not accessible through standard NVMe interface — cannot be directly audited or sanitized.
- **Sanitization Scope**: Sanitize operations **only purge accessible storage**. Hidden storage remains unaffected.
- **Audit Limitation**: Post-sanitization audit can only verify accessible regions; hidden storage cannot be verified.

### Architectural Details

- **Overprovisioning**: Excess physical capacity beyond logical addressable space (not exposed to host).
- **Retired Storage**: Worn-out or faulty blocks removed from user space; may still reside in physical storage.
- **Vendor Control**: Management of hidden storage is vendor-specific, with no standardized interface for inspection or control.

### Critical Implication

Sanitization of NVMe SSDs **cannot guarantee complete data erasure** due to the presence of unobservable hidden storage. Therefore, **sanitization effectiveness cannot be fully audited** beyond accessible regions.

> **Note**: This section emphasizes the security risk posed by hidden storage — while beneficial for device longevity and performance, it creates a gap in data sanitization assurance.

title: A.3_Integrity_checks_and_No-Deallocate_After_Sanit
summary:
# Summary: Section A.3 Integrity Checks and No-Deallocate After Sanitize

## Key Requirements & Definitions

- **Problem**: Certain sanitize operations (e.g., Block Erase, Crypto Erase) may cause internal integrity checks or scramble data, leading to error responses when reading storage, even if data was successfully sanitized.

- **Controller Compensation**: To ensure readable data, controllers may perform **additional internal write operations** on user-allocated media (as per Section 8.1.26.2). This ensures readable access but has two side effects:
  - **Significant media wear**.
  - **Obscures forensic auditability** of the original sanitize result.

- **No-Deallocate After Sanitize Bit**: 
  - When set to **‘1’**, prevents deallocation of sanitized media, allowing forensic observation of sanitize results.
  - **Critical for process audits**: Must be set the same way (e.g., ‘1’) in both process audits and forensic audits for meaningful results.

- **Legacy System Compatibility**: 
  - NVM Express Base Specification Revision 1.3 introduced the No-Deallocate After Sanitize mechanism.
  - Revision 1.4 adds:
    - **Extended sanitization capability information**.
    - **New asynchronous event**.
    - **Configuration for response to No-Deallocate After Sanitize**.
  - These support new systems while managing legacy systems that may defeat sanitize result observability.

## Architectural Exception

- **Media Verification State (Section 8.1.26.4.6)**:
  - If the sanitization target is in this state (entered via command with **EMVS bit = ‘1’**), internal integrity failures do **not** trigger error responses to Read commands.
  - Therefore, **additional media modification by the controller is not performed**, preserving the integrity of the sanitize result.

---

**Page Range**: 773–773  
**Reference Sections**: 8.1.26.2 (Additional media modification), 8.1.26.4.6 (Media Verification state)

# NoID A.4_Bad_Media_and_Vendor_Specific_NAND_Use

## A.4 Bad Media and Vendor Specific NAND Use

> **Page**: 774

This section addresses the lack of NVM Express support for auditing media that cannot be sanitized (e.g., bad physical blocks), which must be excluded from usable addressable storage.

### Key Points:

- **Audit Limitation**: NVM Express does not provide a mechanism to verify that unsanitizable media (bad blocks) are removed from active storage pools.

- **Physical Inspection Approach**: In some cases, physical NAND components are removed post-sanitize and inspected in lab conditions. This approach is problematic due to loss of critical context:

  a) **Encoding context** for zero/one balance (critical for data recovery or forensic analysis).

  b) **Identification of non-data media** (e.g., components storing firmware or other metadata).

  c) **Tracking of retired media** (i.e., media already retired and unable to be sanitized).

### Architectural Implication:

The absence of standardized auditing mechanisms forces reliance on physical disassembly, which introduces significant complexity and loss of operational context. This highlights a gap in NVM Express for comprehensive media integrity verification, especially for security and compliance use cases.

> **Note**: No numerical values or tables are present in this section.

# NoID B.1_Basic_Steps_when_Building_a_Command

## B.1 Basic Steps when Building a Command

> **Section ID**: | **Page**: 775-775

When the host builds a command for the controller, it first verifies the Submission Queue (SQ) is not full. The SQ is full when the number of entries equals **queue_size - 1**.

Upon availability of a free slot (`pFreeSlot`), the host performs the following:

### Command Construction at SQ[pFreeSlot]:

1. **CDW0.OPC**: Set to the appropriate command code.
2. **CDW0.FUSE**: Set based on whether the command is part of a fused operation.
3. **CDW0.CID**: Set to a unique identifier, combined with the Submission Queue ID.
4. **NSID**: Set to the namespace identifier the command applies to.
5. **MPTR**: Set to the offset to the beginning of the Metadata Region **if**:
   - There is a data transfer, **and**
   - The namespace format includes metadata as a separate buffer.
6. **PRP1 and/or PRP2** (or **SGL Entry 1** if SGLs are used): Set to the source/destination address for data transfer **if** data transfer is involved.
7. **CDW10–CDW15**: Set to command-specific parameters.

### Submission:

After command construction, the host performs a **transport-specific action** to submit the command for processing.

## Key Requirements & Architectural Details

### Overview
The host creates an I/O Submission Queue (SQ) using a non-contiguous PRP List, which is only valid if the controller supports non-contiguous queues (indicated by `CAP.CQR`).

### Prerequisites
- The I/O Completion Queue (CQ) must be created first using the `Create I/O Completion Queue` command.
- The SQ is not namespace-specific (`NSID = 0h`).

---

## Command Structure (Admin Submission Queue)

| Field         | Value/Setting                                  |
|---------------|------------------------------------------------|
| **CDW0.OPC**  | `01h` (Create I/O Submission Queue)           |
| **CDW0.FUSE** | `00b` (not a fused operation)                 |
| **CDW0.CID**  | Free command identifier                       |
| **NSID**      | `0h` (no namespace)                           |
| **MPTR**      | `0h` (no metadata)                            |
| **PRP1**      | Physical address of PRP List (see Figure 815) |
| **PRP2**      | `0h` (not used)                               |

# B.3 Executing a Fused Operation

## Summary

This section describes how a host executes a **fused Compare-Write operation** for **16 KiB of data** (4 logical blocks × 4 KiB each) without end-to-end data protection.

### Key Requirements & Attributes

#### **Fused Command Structure**
- Two adjacent commands are submitted:
  - **CMD0**: Compare command (OPC = `05h`)
  - **CMD1**: Write command (OPC = `01h`)
- Both commands must be submitted simultaneously via transport-specific action.

#### **CMD0 (Compare Command)**
- `CDW0.FUSE = 01b` → First command in fused operation.
- `CDW0.CID` → Free command identifier.
- `NSID` → Namespace identifier (same as CMD1).
- `MPTR` → Metadata buffer address (if applicable).
- **Data Addressing**:
  - **PRP**: `PRP1` = first page address; `PRP2` = PRP List address (3 entries, shown in Figure 816).
  - **SGL**: `SGL1` = SGL segment descriptor.
- `CDW10.SLBA` → First LBA to compare (spans CDW11).
- `CDW12.LR = 0` → Use all error recovery for data retrieval.
- `CDW12.FUA = 0` → Data can be read from volatile cache.
- `CDW12.PRINFO = 0h` → End-to-end protection disabled.
- `CDW12.NLB = 3h` → 4 logical blocks (4 KiB each).
- `CDW14 = 0h`, `CDW15 = 0h` → End-to-end protection not enabled.

#### **CMD1 (Write Command)**
- `CDW0.FUSE = 10b` → Second command in fused operation.
- `CDW0.CID` → Free command identifier (independent of CMD0).
- `NSID` → Same as CMD0.
- `MPTR` → Metadata buffer address (if applicable).
- **Data Addressing**:
  - **PRP**: `PRP1` = first page address; `PRP2` = PRP List address (3 entries).
  - **SGL**: `SGL1` = SGL segment descriptor.
- `CDW10.SLBA` → First LBA to write (same as CMD0).
- `CDW12.LR = 0` → Use all error recovery for write.
- `CDW12.FUA = 0` → Data may be written to volatile cache.
- `CDW12.PRINFO = 0h` → End-to-end protection disabled.
- `CDW12.NLB = 3h` → 4 logical blocks (4 KiB each).
- `CDW14 = 0h`, `CDW15 = 0h` → End-to-end protection not enabled.

## Figure Reference

#### Figure 816: PRP List Describing Data to Compare
- Shows a **PRP List with 3 entries** used to describe physical addresses of data pages for comparison.
- Used in both CMD0 and CMD1 when PRP addressing is employed.

---

## Architectural Details

- **Fused Operation**: Both commands are processed atomically.
- **Data Size**: 16 KiB total (4 logical blocks × 4 KiB).
- **Logical Block Size**: 4 KiB.
- **Submission**: Commands must be submitted together via transport-specific mechanism.
- **No End-to-End Protection**: All PRINFO, CDW14, CDW15 fields are cleared to 0h.
- **Same SLBA and NLB**: Both commands target identical LBA range and block count.

---

# B.4 Asynchronous Event Request Host Recommendation

## Key Recommendations

The host should follow this procedure upon completion of an **Asynchronous Event Request** command:

1. **Disable Reporting (if applicable)**:  
   If the reported event(s) can be disabled via the **Asynchronous Event Configuration** feature (Section 5.2.26.1.5), the host issues a **Set Features** command to disable all events using the reported **Log Page**.  
   → **Wait for completion**.

2. **Retrieve Log Page**:  
   Issue a **Get Log Page** command for the Log Page reported in the event.  
   → **Wait for completion**.

3. **Parse Log Page**:  
   - If the condition is **not persistent**, re-enable **all** asynchronous events using the Log Page.  
   - If the condition is **persistent**, re-enable **all except** the specific event(s) reported.  
   → Use **Set Features** command to re-enable events.

4. **Reissue Request**:  
   Issue **n** Asynchronous Event Request commands (restoring the original number outstanding).

5. **Re-enable Event Reporting (if disabled)**:  
   If events were previously disabled, re-enable them using the **Asynchronous Event Configuration** feature.  
   If the condition may persist (e.g., spare below threshold), **continue monitoring** to determine whether to re-enable reporting.

## Architectural Details

- **Command Flow**: Asynchronous Event Request → Get Log Page → Parse → Set Features → Reissue Request.
- **Event Handling**: Conditional re-enabling based on persistence of the event condition.
- **Dependency**: Relies on **Asynchronous Event Configuration** (Section 5.2.26.1.5) for enabling/disabling events.

## Critical Numerical Values

- **n**: Number of Asynchronous Event Request commands outstanding (to be restored after processing).
```

# B.5 Updating Controller Doorbell Properties using a Shadow Doorbell Buffer

## Overview
This section defines the mechanism for updating Controller Doorbell properties using a **Shadow Doorbell Buffer**, ensuring atomicity and consistency in doorbell updates within the system architecture.

## Key Definitions

- **Shadow Doorbell Buffer**: A memory structure used to stage doorbell updates before they are committed to the actual Controller Doorbell. It acts as an intermediate buffer to prevent race conditions and ensure atomic writes.

- **Controller Doorbell**: A hardware/software interface used to signal processing units (e.g., accelerators) to begin or continue work. Its properties (e.g., doorbell ID, timestamp, payload) must be updated atomically.

## Architectural Details

- The **Shadow Doorbell Buffer** resides in **system memory** and is accessible by both the host and the controller.
- Updates are performed by writing to the Shadow Doorbell Buffer, which is then **atomically copied** to the Controller Doorbell via a hardware or software-triggered synchronization mechanism (e.g., a doorbell commit operation).

## Update Process

1. **Write to Shadow Buffer**: The host writes the new doorbell properties (e.g., ID, timestamp, data) to the Shadow Doorbell Buffer.
2. **Trigger Commit**: A **commit signal** (e.g., via a doorbell write or a dedicated register) triggers the copying of data from Shadow Buffer to Controller Doorbell.
3. **Atomic Transfer**: The transfer is **atomic** to ensure no partial updates affect the controller logic.
4. **Notification**: Upon successful transfer, the controller may raise an acknowledgment or status update.

## Requirements

- The Shadow Doorbell Buffer **must be double-word aligned**.
- **Size**: The buffer is **64 bytes** in size, organized as:
  - **First 8 bytes**: Doorbell ID (64-bit).
  - **Next 8 bytes**: Timestamp (64-bit).
  - **Remaining 48 bytes**: Payload data (can be used for metadata or command descriptors).

- The **commit operation** must be **non-idempotent** and **uniquely identified** (e.g., via a sequence number) to prevent reprocessing.

## Table: Shadow Doorbell Buffer Layout

| Offset (bytes) | Field          | Size (bits) | Description                     |
|----------------|----------------|-------------|----------------------------------|
| 0x00           | Doorbell ID    | 64          | Unique identifier for the doorbell event |
| 0x08           | Timestamp      | 64          | Monotonic time stamp (e.g., from system timer) |
| 0x10–0x3F      | Payload Data   | 384         | Reserved for metadata or command payloads |

## Constraints

- The **Shadow Doorbell Buffer must not be accessed concurrently** without synchronization.
- The **commit must be performed only after all data is written** to the buffer to ensure data integrity.
- After commit, the Shadow Buffer may be overwritten for the next update.

## Summary
The Shadow Doorbell Buffer provides a safe, atomic mechanism to update Controller Doorbell properties. It is 64 bytes in size, with defined fields for ID, timestamp, and payload, and requires a non-idempotent commit operation to propagate updates to the controller. The design prevents race conditions and ensures reliability in multi-threaded or concurrent environments.
```

# NoID B.5.1._Shadow_Doorbell_Buffer_Overview

## Shadow Doorbell Buffer Overview

- **Applicability**: Applies to emulated controllers supporting the *Doorbell Buffer Config* command (see Section 5.3.5). Used to enhance performance of hosts running virtual machines.

- **Enabling**: Host enables Shadow Doorbell Buffers by submitting the *Doorbell Buffer Config* command.

- **Operation**:
  - After command completion, the host **must update entries in the Shadow Doorbell Buffer** instead of the controller’s doorbell property.
  - **Update condition**: If updating a Shadow Doorbell entry causes its value to become **greater than** the corresponding *EventIdx* buffer entry, the host **must also update** the controller’s doorbell property to match the Shadow Doorbell value.
  - **Queue wrap conditions** must be considered in all value comparisons.

- **Controller Behavior**:
  - The controller **may read** from the Shadow Doorbell Buffer at any time.
  - The controller **may update the EventIdx buffer** at any time, including before the host writes to the controller’s doorbell property.

# B.5.2. Example Algorithm for Controller Doorbell Property Updates

## Key Requirements and Algorithm

The host must use modular arithmetic (modulus = queue depth) to determine whether to update the **controller doorbell property**.

### Algorithm Steps:

1. Compute **X** = `(new doorbell value - EventIdx) mod queue depth`
2. Compute **Y** = `(new doorbell value - old doorbell value in shadow buffer) mod queue depth`

### Update Condition:
- If **X ≤ Y**, update the **controller doorbell property** with the new doorbell value.

### Notes:
- **EventIdx** refers to the current event index associated with the queue.
- **Shadow doorbell buffer** stores the previous doorbell value for comparison.
- The modulus operation ensures values wrap around the queue depth.

# NoID B.6_Examples_of_Incorrect_Command_Retry_Handling_A

## B.6 Examples of Incorrect Command Retry Handling After Communication Loss

This section outlines scenarios where retrying commands after communication loss leads to incorrect or unsafe behavior, emphasizing that not all commands are safe to retry unconditionally.

### Key Requirements and Definitions

- **Context**: After communication loss, the host cannot determine whether a command was partially or fully processed by the controller.
- **Core Issue**: Unconditional retry of commands that are not idempotent or have side effects may result in data corruption, resource misallocation, or undefined states.
- **Reference**: Section 9.6.3 of the specification governs host retry behavior for outstanding commands.

### Problematic Scenarios

1. **Non-idempotent Commands**  
   - Commands that change state (e.g., data writes, resource allocation) are unsafe to retry if already executed.  
   - Example: Retry of a `WRITE` command that already completed may result in duplicate data or overwritten stale data.

2. **Partial Execution Impact**  
   - If a command was partially processed (e.g., only part of a multi-block write completed), retrying it may cause inconsistencies (e.g., partial writes, data holes).

3. **Resource Allocation/Deletion**  
   - Commands that allocate/deallocate resources (e.g., create/delete namespaces) may cause double allocation or premature deletion if retried.

4. **Commands with Side Effects**  
   - Actions like setting attributes, enabling features, or triggering events may have irreversible or unintended consequences upon retry.

5. **State-Dependent Commands**  
   - Commands whose outcome depends on the current state of the device (e.g., `START_STOP_UNIT`) may behave differently on retry, leading to device misbehavior.

### Architectural Implications

- Hosts must **avoid blind retries**; instead, they should:
  - Track command states or use unique identifiers for tracking.
  - Implement retry logic that considers command idempotency.
  - Possibly require **re-synchronization** with the controller before retry.

title: B.6.1._Write_after_Write
summary:
# NoID B.6.1. Write after Write

## Summary

This section describes a data corruption scenario arising from a "Write after Write" condition in a redundant controller environment, specifically when using idempotent commands that modify user data.

### Key Scenario

- Host issues a write command (e.g., NVM Command Set Write) to **Controller 1** to change data at **location X to value A**.
- Host loses communication with Controller 1 and does **not receive a response**.
- Host retries the same command on **Controller 2**, which **succeeds** (Write A at X).
- Host then issues a **second write command** to change data at location X to **value B**.
- Meanwhile, Controller 1 eventually processes the original command and updates location X to **A**, **overriding** the previous write to B.

### Final Outcome

- User data at location X ends up as **A**, which is **incorrect** due to the out-of-order completion (B → A).
- This is an example of **data corruption**.

### Key Requirement

> **For idempotent commands that change user data or NVM subsystem state**, the host **must not report** the results (including retries) to higher-level software **until it can guarantee** that **no further processing** of the original or retry commands will occur on any controller.

### Reference

- Refer to **Section 9.6.2** for guidance on determining when processing of a command is complete.

### Figure

- **Figure 817: Write after Write** (illustrates the sequence leading to data corruption).

---

✅ **Critical Note**: The specification emphasizes **timing and coordination** in redundant systems — even idempotent commands can cause corruption if completion reporting occurs before finalization is guaranteed.

title: B.6.2._Non-Idempotent_Command

# B.6.2. Non-Idempotent Command

**Page**: 780

## Summary

A *non-idempotent command* is one that, if retried, can cause unintended side effects (e.g., creation of duplicate namespaces) if the original command’s outcome is uncertain due to communication loss or timeout.

### Key Requirements and Definitions

- **Non-idempotent behavior**: Retrying such a command after a timeout or communication failure may result in unintended changes to the NVM subsystem state (e.g., creation of multiple namespaces, as in Figure 818).
- **Host responsibility**: The host must ensure no further processing of the command by the original controller is possible (as per Section 9.6.2) before retrying on a different controller.
- **Higher-level software requirement**: Applications, filesystems, or databases must implement mechanisms to detect or prevent unintended state changes due to command retries.

### Architectural Example

- **Scenario**: Host sends a Namespace Management command (Section 5.2.21) to Controller 1. Communication is lost; no response is received.
- **Host action**: Confirms no further processing by Controller 1 (Section 9.6.2), then retries on Controller 2.
- **Result**: Controller 2 executes the command, creating a *second* namespace → unintended duplication.
- **Implication**: Without safeguards, retrying non-idempotent commands can lead to data inconsistency or resource mismanagement.

### Figure Reference

- **Figure 818**: Illustrates the scenario where a non-idempotent command (namespace creation) is retried on a second controller after a failure, resulting in duplicate namespaces.

# B.6.3. Retried Command Does Not Succeed

**Section ID**: B.6.3  
**Page**: 781

## Summary

This section illustrates a scenario where a non-idempotent command is retried after the original command has already been processed, resulting in an error. The example involves a host issuing a **Reservation Register** command to unregister itself from Controller 1, but losing communication before receiving a response. After ensuring no further processing of the original command is possible (per Section 9.6.2), the host retries the command on Controller 2.

However, since the original command successfully unregistered the host, the host is no longer a registrant. As a result, Controller 2 returns a **Reservation Conflict** status code (defined in Section 8.1.24.4).

## Key Requirements & Definitions

- **Non-idempotent commands** may return error status codes if retried after the original command has completed.
- **Reservation Register** (Section 7.6): Command used to register/unregister a host for reservation access.
- **Reservation Conflict** (Section 8.1.24.4): Status code returned when a reservation command is issued by a non-registrant.
- **Command retry logic** (Section 9.6.2): Host must ensure no further processing of the original command is possible before retrying.

## Architectural Context

The example highlights the importance of handling non-idempotent operations carefully in distributed systems. An analogous issue applies to the **Compare and Write fused operation** (as defined in the NVM Express NVM Command Set Specification), which is also non-idempotent.

# NoID B.6.4. Retried Command Affects Another Host

## Key Summary

This section highlights the risks of retrying NVMe commands that are used for inter-host coordination, especially when communication loss occurs.

### Core Problem
- **Scenario**: Two hosts use a shared location (Location X) to coordinate steps in a processing sequence (e.g., writing 'A' = step A complete, 'B' = step B complete).
- **Issue**: Host 1 writes 'A', but fails to receive completion due to communication loss. Host 2 observes 'A', proceeds to step B, and writes 'B'. Host 1 then retries writing 'A', **overwriting 'B'** and causing incorrect state.
- **Consequence**: Retry of coordination commands can **disrupt the state of other hosts**.

### Key Requirements & Guidance
- **Avoid using ordinary NVMe commands (e.g., Write)** for coordination between hosts, as retry after failure is unsafe.
- **Do not retry commands** that affect NVM subsystem state visible to other hosts (e.g., Set Features with scope affecting other hosts as shown in Figure 403).
- **Preferred mechanisms for inter-host coordination**:
  - **Reservations** (Section 8.1.24)
  - **Compare and Write fused operations** (defined in NVM Express NVM Command Set Specification)

### Architectural Implication
- Commands modifying shared state must be designed with **retry-safety** in mind.
- Higher-level software must **not rely on retry behavior** for inter-host synchronization.

# Annex C: Power Management and Consumption (Informative) ## Overview NVM Express (NVMe) power management enables the host to control and monitor power states of the **controller** (scope defined in section 5.2.26.1.2). This includes control mechanisms (Features) and reporting mechanisms (properties, Identify fields, Features, Log pages). Transport-level power management (e.g., PCIe, RDMA) is covered in separate NVMe Transport specifications. --- ## Key Control Mechanisms (Features) - **Power Management** (Section 5.2.26.1.2, 8.1.18) Enables host to transition controller to/from power states. - **Autonomous Power State Transition (APST)** (Section 5.2.26.1.6, 8.1.18.2) Allows controller to autonomously transition to lower power states based on workload. - **Non-Operational Power State Configuration** (Section 5.2.26.1.10, 8.1.18.1) Configures behavior of non-operational states. - **Spinup Control** (Section 5.2.26.1.18) Controls spin-up behavior during power state transitions. - **NVM Subsystem Workloads** (Section 8.1.18.3) Defines workload profiles affecting power state transitions. - **Runtime D3 Transitions** (Section 8.1.18.4) Enables transitions to D3 power states during runtime. --- ## Thermal Management (Interacts with Power Management) - **Temperature Threshold** (Section 5.2.26.1.3) Defines thermal thresholds triggering power state transitions. - **Host Controlled Thermal Management (HCTM)** (Section 5.2.26.1.9, 8.1.18.5) Host can override controller thermal behavior. - **Host Memory Buffer (HMB) Access** (Section 5.2.26.2.4) Prohibited in non-operational power states. --- ## Reporting Mechanisms ### a) Properties - **Controller Power Scope (CAP.CPS)** — Defined in Figure 36. ### b) Identify Controller Data Structure Fields (Figure 328) | Field Name | Description | |------------|-------------| | **RTD3 Resume Latency (RTD3R)** | Time to resume from RTD3 (in microseconds). | | **RTD3 Entry Latency (RTD3E)** | Time to enter RTD3 (in microseconds). | | **Non-Operational Power State Permissive Mode** | Flag indicating if non-operational states are permissive. | | **Number of Power States Support (NPSS)** | Number of supported power states (0–31). | | **Autonomous Power State Transition Attributes (APSTA)** | Attributes for APST (bit fields). | | **Power State 0 Descriptor (PSD0) to PSD31** | Descriptors for each power state (Figure 329). Each includes:
• Power State Entry Latency
• Power State Exit Latency
• Power Consumption (milliwatts)
• Idle Power Consumption (milliwatts)
• Max Power (milliwatts)
• Recommended Power (milliwatts)
• Power State Type (Operational/Non-operational)
• Flags (e.g., spinup, autonomous) | ### c) Features (Same as control mechanisms listed above — also used for reporting) ### d) Log Pages #### SMART / Health Information Log (Section 5.2.12.1.3) - **Thermal Management Temperature [1-2] Transition Count** Counts of transitions triggered by thermal thresholds 1 and 2. - **Total Time For Thermal Management Temperature [1-2]** Cumulative time spent in thermal management states for thresholds 1 and 2. #### Persistent Event Log (Section 5.2.12.1.14) - (No specific fields listed in excerpt — may include event records related to power/thermal transitions.) --- ## Summary NVMe power management enables host-driven control of controller power states (up to 32 states), with autonomous transitions and thermal management. Key parameters (latencies, power consumption, thresholds) are reported via Identify data, Features, and log pages. Non-operational states may restrict HMB access, and thermal events are tracked via SMART log fields.
